intro: E major replaces the first movement’s C-minor centre, and long string and wind phrases replace its persistent rhythmic pressure. Follow the oboe melody towards its later return with horn and solo violin.
question: How does changing the instruments change a returning melody?

sections.label: A · strings and oboe
sections.mNote: a string phrase opens into a second, oboe-led melody

sections.label: B · unsettled middle
sections.mNote: dotted rhythms and displaced accents disturb the three-beat pulse

sections.label: A′ · the opening transformed
sections.mNote: winds foreground the opening phrase; strings add moving accompaniment

sections.label: A′ · oboe, horn and solo violin
sections.mNote: the second opening melody returns in a new instrumental combination

sections.label: Coda · the solo line remains
sections.mNote: horn melody and violin decoration extend the E-major close

cues.title: Strings before the oboe
cues.text: The opening phrase belongs to the strings, with bassoon doubling the violin melody. Its rising and falling line includes a long–short dotted rhythm. The oboe’s better-known melody comes later within this opening section.
cues.evidence: The first-edition score p. 27 shows strings and bassoon at the opening, followed by the oboe-led second melody at bar 18. The report begins at a restrained level, with a first marked change around 0:18; no exact later oboe entry is asserted.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Semitones inside the song
cues.text: Across the opening, listen for small rising semitone steps within the longer melody. The first movement’s insistence has become part of a sustained phrase, while lower-string triplets give the accompaniment its own motion.
cues.evidence: Simrock p. 27, especially bars 5–17, shows rising chromatic figures and cello triplets. This is a general opening-section observation; the analysis does not identify individual inner parts.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A wind line comes forward
cues.text: In the later part of the opening section, an oboe carries a more expansive melody. Listen for its connection to the strings’ earlier dotted rhythms: the change of colour does not require wholly unrelated material.
cues.evidence: Bar 18 introduces the oboe melody; its approximate region here is 1:05–1:30, before the opening section closes near 1:46. The report has a relatively steady lower-level stretch at 1:00–1:20 and a rise around 1:25; instrument identity comes from the score.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The middle unsettles the metre
cues.text: The middle section keeps dotted rhythms but lets the accents slip away from the expected downbeat. Listen for the tension between the written three-beat measure and phrases that seem to begin in the wrong place.
cues.evidence: The score’s B section begins at bar 28 with dotted and syncopated figures. The 1:46 boundary precedes a brighter, more active stretch at 1:50–2:15; this supports the approximate 106-second join.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A melody across displaced beats
cues.text: Through the central wind phrases, try following the sustained melody separately from the off-beat string gestures. The parts do not always point to the same downbeat; that disagreement makes the line less settled than its smooth surface suggests.
cues.evidence: Bars 39–48 place oboe and then clarinet above syncopated strings. The report’s lower-level stretch at 2:30–3:00 follows the middle section’s first swell; this locates a passage, not either soloist’s first note.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An orchestral work without a soloist
cues.text: This symphony names no concerto soloist, yet its slow movement gives individual players chamber-like prominence. The first edition separates a solo violin from the first-violin section in the later return; that player remains a distinct voice into the coda.
cues.evidence: The orchestral score and Hansen’s bar descriptions identify the solo violin from bar 91 through the close: http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html. The observation concerns the movement’s scoring and genre, not a violin entry at 3:10.

cues.title: The middle crest subsides
cues.text: The central section reaches a broad swell, then loses much of its weight. Listen through the withdrawal: the return of the opening will be a reorganisation of the texture, not simply another loud arrival.
cues.evidence: Relative level is high at 3:30–3:50, then falls to −23.6 dB at 3:55 and −32.8 at 4:00. The feature supports the retreat leading towards the score-proportional return near 4:04.

cues.title: The opening changes hands
cues.text: In the return, winds take a more prominent role in the opening theme while the strings add motion around them. Listen for a familiar melodic outline inside unfamiliar accompaniment: recognition depends on the phrase, not on repeating its original colour.
cues.evidence: Bar 67 begins the varied return, with the theme in winds and added string figuration. The report recovers from its 4:00 low point into an E-centred stretch at 4:05–4:25; 244 seconds is an approximate sectional anchor.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Clara as a musical reader
cues.text: Clara Schumann heard and criticised Brahms’s new music across more than forty years of friendship. Her response to this symphony was not unreserved: she found the finale’s brilliant ending less convincing than its earlier music.
cues.evidence: The site’s Brahms biography documents Clara’s continuing musical role. Mandel quotes her reservation about the finale in the Boston Symphony note: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: One melody, three colours
cues.text: In the later return of the oboe melody, horn and solo violin join its line. Compare this mixed colour with the oboe’s earlier statement; the violin’s separate voice will continue after the shared melody has passed.
cues.evidence: The score combines oboe, horn and solo violin from bar 91. Strong changes at 5:36 and 5:48, followed by the swell at 5:55–6:15, support approximate placement around 5:48. No individual entry is claimed within two seconds.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return does not mean repetition
cues.text: The returning phrases alter their accompaniment and their route to the cadence. Listen for the melody remaining recognisable while plucked triplets and small answering figures keep its surroundings in motion.
cues.evidence: Bars 91–100 retain the second melody but add solo violin, horn, imitative accompaniment and plucked cello triplets. The report’s 5:55–6:15 swell gives way at 6:20 before the coda region; this is a passage comparison.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The coda decorates the melody
cues.text: The coda gives the horn the melodic foreground while the solo violin adds more mobile decoration. Keep the sustained line and its ornament separate in your attention; one can hold the phrase together while the other fills its spaces.
cues.evidence: Bars 101–104 place the horn theme beneath decorative solo violin. The coda is estimated around 6:32 from the score’s proportions and the E-major, more active stretch at 6:30–6:50; later phrases continue this solo texture.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A public-domain recording project
cues.text: This performance belongs to the Musopen Kickstarter collection, released in 2012. Commons and the upstream archive credit the Czech National Symphony Orchestra. Neither names the conductor or identifies the session date; the release year is not presented as a recording date.
cues.evidence: Commons identifies the ensemble and Musopen source; the upstream collection describes its 2012 completion: https://archive.org/metadata/MusopenCollectionAsFlac. The dossier distinguishes collection release from an unestablished session.

cues.title: The last line outlasts its support
cues.text: In the written ending, the solo violin holds its final note across the orchestra’s quiet chord repetitions. Listen for that sustained upper line rather than treating every chord as a fresh melodic beginning.
cues.evidence: The score’s closing bars 123–128 sustain the solo violin while accompaniment reiterates the harmony. The report remains E-centred through 8:30 and falls to −57.4 dB at 8:35; the release itself is not precisely aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The cadence releases displaced dotted rhythms
transitions.how: An E-major cadence ends the opening section, but its arrival also launches the next phrase. Violins carry a lilting dotted rhythm onwards, and the other strings answer with displaced accents and semitone motion. The middle section grows from the existing long–short rhythm rather than a new tempo marking; changing accents and a turn towards minor make the continuity unstable.
transitions.evidence: The written join is bar 28. The report has a boundary at 1:46, followed by increased brightness and activity at 1:50–2:15. E major and the dotted-rhythm continuation come from the score, not automatic chord labels.

transitions.title: Overlapping phrases restore the opening
transitions.how: The middle section’s retreat leads to overlapping rising and falling figures that continue to obscure the three-beat metre. A quiet timpani roll supports the preparation. The opening theme returns in the winds, while strings add a sweeping line and plucked triplets. The recovered E-major centre is therefore paired with altered orchestration rather than an unchanged replay of the opening.
transitions.evidence: Bars 63–67 supply the retransition and wind-led return. Relative level falls towards the 4:00 minimum, then rises at 4:05; score proportions place the return near 244 seconds, without bar alignment.

transitions.title: A cadence opens the melody’s new colour
transitions.how: The varied opening section reaches a B-major cadence, whose arrival overlaps the second melody’s upbeat. The music turns back towards E major while oboe, horn and solo violin combine on the familiar tune. Plucked cello triplets and answering figures in other parts provide movement underneath; the melody’s new colour comes from adding independent players, not from thickening every orchestral line.
transitions.evidence: Bar 91 is the score reference for the second melody’s return and solo combination. The report’s 5:36 and 5:48 changes precede the 5:55–6:15 swell; 348 seconds is a passage estimate.

transitions.title: An unfinished cadence leaves the soloists speaking
transitions.how: The returning melody approaches a cadence but continues into a coda before its upper parts complete the expected close. Horn states the melody’s opening gestures while the solo violin decorates them. Triplet figures and a sustained tonic foundation keep E major present without making each bar a fresh arrival. The solo writing extends the phrase beyond the formal return.
transitions.evidence: Bars 97–104 describe the incomplete cadential continuation into the coda. The report withdraws at 6:20 and becomes E-centred with increased activity at 6:30–6:50; 392 seconds is estimated, not a measured instrument entrance.

source.title: Brahms, Symphony No. 1, Simrock first-edition full score, plate 7957 (1877)
source.locator: Movement II, pp. 27–34; opening inspected directly. Later representative textures use Hansen’s score descriptions at bars 28, 39, 67, 91, 101 and 123. Timings are approximate snapshots derived from this recording’s analysis, not continuous player tracking.

timeline.note: The opening melody is in strings, doubled by bassoon; horns answer within the phrase.
The opening section’s second melody foregrounds oboe with wind harmony and light viola support.
The middle begins with lilting dotted string figures that acquire syncopation and weight.
Central oboe and clarinet phrases pass above off-beat upper-string accompaniment.
The varied return puts the opening melody into winds while strings supply sweeping and plucked motion.
Oboe, horn and solo violin share the second melody above an enriched accompaniment.
In the coda, the horn carries melodic gestures while solo violin adds decoration.
The closing passage retains the solo violin’s sustained note above quiet chord repetitions.

facts: Piano with Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel; piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen in Hamburg
Seasonal work in Detmold, 1857–59; Vienna Singakademie, 1863–64; Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde concerts, 1872–75
Based in Vienna; summer composition in Baden-Baden, Pörtschach, Mürzzuschlag and Bad Ischl
Four symphonies, four concertos, chamber music, piano music, songs and choral works; no opera
composer.background:
Brahms was born in Hamburg, the son of a professional musician, Johann Jakob Brahms, who played several instruments, and Christiane Nissen, a seamstress. His father supplied an introduction to practical music-making; Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel and Eduard Marxsen gave him systematic piano and composition lessons. The young Brahms played for income and learned the trade from inside, accompanying, arranging and performing. Marxsen’s teaching connected keyboard technique with the study of Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. Those composers supplied working materials: Brahms’s later scores are full of old procedures subjected to new rhythmic pressure.

In 1853 he toured with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi and met Joseph Joachim, who became a lifelong collaborator. Joachim sent him to Robert and Clara Schumann in Düsseldorf. Robert’s article “Neue Bahnen”, published that October, announced the twenty-year-old as a major new figure before his music was widely available. The endorsement opened publishers’ doors and imposed an awkward expectation of scale. His early piano sonatas, already orchestral in weight and contrast, could be treated as promises of symphonies he had not yet written. Brahms responded by publishing selectively and destroying much of the work he did not wish to preserve.
composer.epithet: A composer who made a small interval generate a large form, and let conflicting rhythms keep a familiar melody unsettled.
